title: Year 10 History — Yearly Exam
exam_focus: Follows the Yearly Assessment Notification: Section One's seven terms (unipolarity, collective security, pre-emption, unilateralism, humanitarian intervention, multilateral, unilateral) plus Section Two's essay "Explain the development of US foreign policy between 1991 and 2019" in three parts (four 1990s events / 9-11, the Bush Doctrine and Iraq / the rise of China and the shift from unipolar to multipolar), with practice writing body paragraphs.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines unipolarity?
options: Power is shared between two rival blocs that balance each other
Power is dispersed among several competing great powers
One state is dominant, with no rival of comparable power
Power rests with whichever state acts first without consulting others
questions.explanation_en: A unipolar system has only one dominant power centre with no peer rivals, whereas bipolarity refers to the Cold War's US-Soviet balance, and multipolarity refers to multiple balancing powers; 'Power rests with whichever state acts first without consulting others' describes unilateralism, not the power structure.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Section One(Unipolarity)

questions.stem: Which action is the clearest example of multilateral action?
options: A coalition of states acting together under UN Security Council authorisation
One state acting alone without notifying any other government
One state threatening to act alone unless its allies fall into line
Two neighbouring states signing a border and trade agreement
questions.explanation_en: Multilateral refers to actions involving multiple countries, usually coordinated through international institutions, with the key phrase being 'multiple countries + authorisation'; 'One state acting alone without notifying any other government' and 'One state threatening to act alone unless its allies fall into line' are unilateral, while 'Two neighbouring states signing a border and trade agreement' is bilateral, not multilateral.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Section One(Multilateral)

questions.stem: A government repeatedly insists it will act alone when allies disagree, even at the cost of isolation. This pattern of behaviour is best described as:
options: Collective security — allies respond together
Multilateralism — several states act together
Humanitarian intervention — force to protect civilians
Unilateralism — the habit of acting alone by choice
questions.explanation_en: Unilateralism is a preference or habit where a country takes action alone despite knowing its allies oppose it, which is the opposite of collective security and multilateralism.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Section One(Unilateralism)

questions.stem: Which statement best defines collective security?
options: Each state builds enough weapons to deter rivals without any allies
States agree that an attack on one member is an attack on all
A powerful state intervenes inside another to stop human rights abuses
A single state decides when and where military force will be used
questions.explanation_en: Collective security rests on the principle that an attack on one country is an attack on all, with members responding together, usually through the United Nations. Self-deterrence, humanitarian intervention and unilateral decision-making are different concepts.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Section One(Collective Security)

questions.stem: Which action is the clearest example of collective security rather than humanitarian intervention?
options: A UN-authorised coalition repelling Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait
NATO aircraft bombing Serbia in 1999 to stop ethnic cleansing
US-led forces invading Iraq in 2003 without any explicit UN approval
US troops landing in Somalia in 1992 to protect food convoys
questions.explanation_en: The Gulf War is the classic example of collective security, because it responded to cross-border aggression. The other examples were driven by protecting civilians or overthrowing a regime, which makes them humanitarian intervention or pre-emption, not collective security.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 1(Gulf War 1991)

questions.stem: In the Bush Doctrine, pre-emption means:
options: Waiting for an attack, then responding with UN approval
Intervening to stop a government killing its own citizens
Working through alliances so no single state decides on war
Striking first at a state or group judged to pose a future threat
questions.explanation_en: Pre-emption involves taking military action before a threat materialises, which is a key difference between the Bush Doctrine and collective security or humanitarian intervention.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Section One(Pre-emption)

questions.stem: Which feature most clearly separates pre-emption from humanitarian intervention?
options: Pre-emption always needs UN authorisation; intervention never does
Pre-emption is always multilateral; intervention is always unilateral in form
Pre-emption answers a future threat; intervention answers harm under way
Pre-emption targets only non-state groups; intervention only states
questions.explanation_en: The key distinction lies in the timing of the threat: pre-emption targets threats that have not yet occurred, while humanitarian intervention responds to ongoing large-scale harm.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Section One(Pre-emption / Humanitarian Intervention)

questions.stem: Which statement best defines humanitarian intervention?
options: Military action to seize disputed territory and its natural resources
Military action inside a state, without consent, to stop mass suffering
Economic sanctions agreed by a regional trade or security organisation
Defensive action taken after a direct attack on one's own soil
questions.explanation_en: Humanitarian intervention has three requirements: entering another country, without their consent, and aiming to stop a large-scale humanitarian disaster, which is different from economic sanctions or self-defence.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Section One(Humanitarian Intervention)

questions.stem: In 2003 State A went to war with a small group of allies after failing to win UN Security Council support, while State B sent troops to a UN-authorised mission. Which pairing is correct?
options: A — unilateral action; B — multilateral action
A — multilateral action; B — unilateral action
A — collective security; B — humanitarian intervention
A — humanitarian intervention; B — collective security
questions.explanation_en: The criterion for judgement is whether there is widespread authorisation: A is unilateral as it involves a small group of allies and bypasses the UN Security Council, while B is multilateral as it involves a UN- authorised mission.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 2(invasion of Iraq)

questions.stem: Why does the course list both 'unilateral' and 'unilateralism' as separate terms?
options: They are synonyms, listed twice for emphasis in the notes
'Unilateral' describes economic policy; 'unilateralism' military policy
'Unilateralism' describes one action; 'unilateral' a whole doctrine
'Unilateral' is one action taken alone; 'unilateralism' is the doctrine
questions.explanation_en: Unilateral refers to a single action taken by one party, while unilateralism refers to a policy or ideology that tends towards solo actions, and understanding this distinction is crucial for Section One.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Section One(Unilateral / Unilateralism)

questions.stem: Body 1 of the essay covers the 1990s. Name the two events from the notification's list that you would use, and justify your choice in one sentence. (2 marks)
questions.answer: The Gulf War (1991) and Somalia (1992–94). Together they show the two ends of the decade: a UN-authorised, broadly multilateral success, and a humanitarian mission whose failure produced a rapid US withdrawal and shaped later reluctance to intervene.
questions.explanation_en: Body 1 needs only two events, but they must contrast rather than simply be listed: one successful multilateral example and one that exposes its limits — the Gulf War and Somalia, or the Gulf War and Kosovo.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 1(possible events)

criteria.t: Names two relevant 1990s events from the notification's list (e.g. the Gulf War 1991 with Somalia 1992–94, or the Gulf War with Kosovo 1999)
Justifies the choice in one sentence by saying what the pair shows (a broadly multilateral UN-authorised success against a mission that exposed the limits of intervention)

questions.stem: Explain how the Gulf War of 1991 demonstrates multilateralism. (2 marks)
questions.answer: The United States led a broad coalition of states acting with United Nations Security Council authorisation to reverse Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, so the response was collectively authorised and its costs and risks were shared rather than carried by one state.
questions.explanation_en: Multilateralism has two key features: UN authorisation and several countries sharing the burden. Answers must explain who authorised the action, how many parties took part and why it counts as multilateral, rather than just saying that many countries were involved.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 1(Gulf War 1991)

criteria.t: States that the United States led a broad coalition of states acting with United Nations Security Council authorisation against Iraq's invasion of Kuwait
Explains that the response was therefore collectively authorised, with costs and risks shared rather than carried by one state

questions.topic: Essay · Gulf War as collective security
questions.stem: Explain why the Gulf War of 1991 is better described as collective security than as humanitarian intervention. (3 marks)
questions.answer: The war responded to a cross-border act of aggression — Iraq's invasion and annexation of Kuwait — and was authorised collectively against that aggression. Its purpose was to restore Kuwait's sovereignty and the regional order, not to protect civilians from their own government, which is the trigger that defines humanitarian intervention.
questions.explanation_en: The key distinction is the trigger: collective security responds to state-on-state aggression, while humanitarian intervention responds to a government harming its own people, with the Gulf War being an example of the former and the late 1990s Kosovo crisis being a controversial example of the latter.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Section One + Body 1

criteria.t: Explains that the war responded to a cross-border act of aggression (Iraq's invasion and annexation of Kuwait) and was authorised collectively against that aggression
Explains that its purpose was to restore Kuwait's sovereignty and the regional order, not to protect civilians from their own government
Contrasts this with the trigger that defines humanitarian intervention (a government harming its own people), which is why the war belongs to collective security

questions.topic: Essay · Somalia and limits of intervention
questions.stem: What did the US experience in Somalia (1992–94) reveal about the limits of humanitarian intervention? (3 marks)
questions.answer: A humanitarian mission to protect food relief expanded into peace enforcement and fighting with local militias, and the deaths of US soldiers in 1993 led to a rapid withdrawal. It showed that without clear objectives and local consent, casualties can end an intervention before it stabilises the country.
questions.explanation_en: Somalia is often used to show that intervention can be easy to start but hard to end: the mission's objective grew from delivering food aid to combat, casualties created domestic pressure, and the result was withdrawal. Answers must set out that causal chain clearly to score full marks.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 1 (Somalia 1992-94) + syllabus supplement

criteria.t: Explains that a humanitarian mission to protect food relief expanded into peace enforcement and fighting with local militias
Explains that the deaths of US soldiers in 1993 led to a rapid withdrawal
Explains the lesson drawn: without clear objectives and local consent, casualties can end an intervention before it stabilises the country

questions.stem: Why is Rwanda (1994) usually described as a failure of humanitarian intervention? (3 marks)
questions.answer: The genocide of Tutsi and moderate Hutu civilians was carried out while the international community had a small, under-resourced peacekeeping force on the ground and refused to reinforce it or even to describe the killings as genocide. The world stood aside, so the decade's humanitarian language was not matched by action.
questions.explanation_en: To answer 'failure' requires two aspects: insufficient on-the-ground power and a lack of willingness to intervene in global politics (even avoiding the term 'genocide'). This contrasts with the proactive intervention in Kosovo around the same time.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 1 (Rwanda 1994) + syllabus supplement

criteria.t: Explains that the genocide of Tutsi and moderate Hutu civilians continued while only a small, under-resourced peacekeeping force was on the ground
Explains that the international community refused to reinforce that force or even to describe the killings as genocide
Explains that the world stood aside, so the decade's humanitarian language was not matched by action

questions.stem: Why is NATO's 1999 intervention in Kosovo often called a 'grey case' of humanitarian intervention? (4 marks)
questions.answer: The motive was genuinely humanitarian — halting the ethnic cleansing of Kosovar Albanians — but NATO acted without explicit UN Security Council authorisation, so the intervention was of questionable legality while being widely seen as legitimate. It therefore sits between a legitimate humanitarian rescue and a unilateral use of force by an alliance.
questions.explanation_en: The term 'grey' means having a justified motive but lacking authorisation: a separation of legitimacy and justification. To score high, you must discuss both sides, as simply stating 'saved people' or 'illegal' won't suffice.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 1 (Kosovo 1999) + syllabus supplement

criteria.t: Identifies the genuinely humanitarian motive: halting the ethnic cleansing of Kosovar Albanians
Explains that NATO acted without explicit UN Security Council authorisation, so the intervention was of questionable legality
Explains that it was nevertheless widely seen as legitimate
Concludes that it therefore sits between a legitimate humanitarian rescue and a unilateral use of force by an alliance

questions.stem: Write a topic sentence for Body 1 (the 1990s) that directly answers the essay question. (2 marks)
questions.answer: In the 1990s the United States used its position as the world's single superpower to lead broadly multilateral, UN-authorised interventions, but its retreat from Somalia and its inaction over Rwanda exposed the limits of that approach.
questions.explanation_en: A topic sentence must include 'time period + argument', rather than just 'many events in the 1990s'. A good topic sentence also foreshadows tension (multilateral leadership vs limitations) and leaves an interface for the link sentence.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 1(topic sentence row)

criteria.t: Names the period (the 1990s) and makes an arguable claim that directly answers the essay question
Signals the tension the paragraph will develop (multilateral leadership against its limits) instead of merely listing events

questions.stem: Explain how the 9/11 attacks changed the priorities of US foreign policy. (3 marks)
questions.answer: They shifted US priorities from managing the post-Cold War order to a global 'war on terror'. The response included the invasion of Afghanistan in 2001, expanded surveillance and detention powers, much higher defence spending, and a willingness to use force pre-emptively and with limited international authorisation.
questions.explanation_en: The anchor for answering is 'priority shift': from maintaining the post-Cold War order to counter-terrorism. You must write about at least two specific manifestations (Afghanistan, surveillance, military spending, pre-emptive strikes), rather than just stating 'became more aggressive'.
questions.source: Term 4 · Lesson 3.1 9/11 Attacks; Notification — Body 2(Impact of 9/11)

criteria.t: Explains that priorities shifted from managing the post-Cold War order to a global 'war on terror'
Gives specific responses: the invasion of Afghanistan in 2001 and/or expanded surveillance and detention powers
Explains that much higher defence spending and a willingness to use force pre-emptively, with limited international authorisation, followed

questions.stem: Outline the key features of the Bush Doctrine. (3 marks)
questions.answer: Pre-emption — striking first against states or groups judged to pose a future threat; a willingness to act unilaterally when multilateral agreement could not be reached; regime change and the promotion of democracy; and the claim that American security required action beyond UN authorisation.
questions.explanation_en: The four characteristics must be illustrated with corresponding examples: pre-emptive strikes (Iraq), unilateralism (bypassing the UN Security Council), regime change (overthrowing Saddam), and promoting democracy. Simply memorising names without explanation will lose marks.
questions.source: Term 4 · Lesson 3.2 The Bush Doctrine; Notification — Body 2

criteria.t: Outlines pre-emption: striking first against states or groups judged to pose a future threat
Outlines unilateral action: a willingness to act without multilateral agreement and beyond UN authorisation
Outlines regime change and the promotion of democracy as aims of the doctrine

questions.stem: Explain why the 2003 invasion of Iraq is often described as unilateral rather than multilateral. (3 marks)
questions.answer: The United States proceeded with a 'coalition of the willing' after failing to obtain explicit UN Security Council authorisation, and supplied most of the troops and funding itself. Key allies such as France and Germany opposed the war, so it lacked the broad, institutionally authorised coalition that made the 1991 Gulf War multilateral.
questions.explanation_en: The criterion is not 'having allies', but 'having broad authorisation and shared responsibility'. Although the US had allies, its small circle and lack of UN Security Council authorisation mean it is classified as unilateral in the textbook.
questions.source: Term 4 · Lesson 4.2 Iraq; Notification — Body 2(invasion of Iraq)

criteria.t: Explains that the United States proceeded with a 'coalition of the willing' after failing to obtain explicit UN Security Council authorisation
Explains that the United States supplied most of the troops and funding itself, and that key allies such as France and Germany opposed the war
Explains that it therefore lacked the broad, institutionally authorised coalition that made the 1991 Gulf War multilateral

questions.stem: Contrast the multilateralism of the 1991 Gulf War with the unilateralism of the 2003 invasion of Iraq. (4 marks)
questions.answer: In 1991 the United States operated through the UN Security Council, built a large coalition with shared costs, and limited the objective to reversing Iraq's aggression. In 2003 it acted after failing to secure explicit Security Council authorisation, with a smaller ad hoc coalition and US forces dominating, and the objective was regime change and disarmament rather than repelling an attack.
questions.explanation_en: Contrasts must be made in three comparable dimensions: authorisation (present/absent), alliance scale and burden-sharing (broad/narrow), and goals (restoring the status quo/changing the regime). Aligning these three points will ensure a stable score.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 1(Gulf War) + Body 2(Iraq)

criteria.t: Contrasts authorisation: 1991 operated through the UN Security Council, while 2003 proceeded after failing to secure explicit Security Council authorisation
Contrasts the coalition: a large coalition with shared costs in 1991 against a smaller ad hoc coalition dominated by US forces in 2003
Contrasts the objectives: reversing Iraq's aggression and restoring Kuwait in 1991 against regime change and disarmament in 2003
Sustains the comparison across these dimensions, explaining what makes one case multilateral and the other unilateral

questions.stem: Explain how the rise of China challenged unipolarity after 2001. (3 marks)
questions.answer: China's rapid economic growth, its entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001, sustained military modernisation, and initiatives such as the Belt and Road and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank gave it regional and global influence. As a result the United States could no longer act as an unchallenged single pole, especially in the Indo-Pacific.
questions.explanation_en: A unipolar system being challenged means the emergence of near-peer competitors. Answers must provide economic (WTO, scale), military, and institutional initiative evidence, as simply stating 'China has grown stronger' is too vague.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 3 (Rise of China) + syllabus supplement

criteria.t: Explains that China's rapid economic growth and its 2001 entry into the World Trade Organization increased its economic weight
Explains that sustained military modernisation and initiatives such as the Belt and Road and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank extended its regional and global influence
Explains the consequence: the United States could no longer act as an unchallenged single pole, especially in the Indo-Pacific

questions.stem: Explain what a decline in US soft power means, and give one example from the period. (2 marks)
questions.answer: Soft power is influence gained through attraction — culture, values and institutions — rather than through coercion or payment. The Iraq War and the abuse of prisoners at Abu Ghraib damaged America's international reputation in the 2000s, making other states less willing to cooperate.
questions.explanation_en: Soft power refers to attractiveness (culture, values, institutions), as opposed to hard power, which involves coercion through military force or money. Providing examples of a damaged image after 2003 is the most direct approach.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 3 (Decline in US soft power) + syllabus supplement

criteria.t: Defines soft power as influence gained through attraction (culture, values and institutions) rather than through coercion or payment
Gives one valid example of decline from the period (e.g. the Iraq War or the abuse of prisoners at Abu Ghraib damaging America's international reputation in the 2000s)

questions.stem: Explain how the rise of protectionism and deglobalisation shaped US foreign policy after 2008. (2 marks)
questions.answer: The global financial crisis and the loss of manufacturing jobs pushed US policy away from promoting free trade. The United States withdrew from the Trans-Pacific Partnership in 2017 and imposed tariffs on Chinese goods from 2018, so trade became a tool of economic pressure rather than of liberal cooperation.
questions.explanation_en: Protectionism refers to using tariffs and barriers to protect domestic industries, while de-globalisation means weakening trade and investment integration. Answers must provide specific policies (withdrawing from TPP, tariffs on China), otherwise, they are just reiterating definitions.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 3 (protectionism/deglobalisation) + syllabus supplement

criteria.t: Explains that the global financial crisis and the loss of manufacturing jobs pushed US policy away from promoting free trade
Gives specific policy evidence: withdrawal from the Trans-Pacific Partnership in 2017 and tariffs on Chinese goods from 2018, making trade a tool of economic pressure

questions.stem: Explain the shift from unipolarity towards a more multipolar order between 1991 and 2019. (3 marks)
questions.answer: In 1991 the United States was the only superpower, with no economic or military peer. By 2019 China had become a near-peer economically, the European Union and Russia asserted independent positions, and regional powers had more room to act, so influence was more widely distributed even though the United States remained militarily dominant.
questions.explanation_en: Evidence of multipolarisation is 'power diffusion': economic scale approaching parity, rising autonomy of regional powers, and emerging institutional alternatives. Be careful to distinguish between 'military strength remaining dominant' and 'overall power no longer being singularly dominant'.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 3 + syllabus supplement

criteria.t: Explains that in 1991 the United States was the only superpower, with no economic or military peer
Explains that by 2019 China had become a near-peer economically, while the European Union and Russia asserted independent positions
Explains that influence was therefore more widely distributed even though the United States remained militarily dominant

questions.stem: Explain how you would structure Body 2 (9/11 and Iraq) — which events, and what the link sentence must do. (3 marks)
questions.answer: Open with the 9/11 attacks as the trigger, then the Bush Doctrine as the doctrinal response (pre-emption, unilateralism, regime change), then the invasion of Iraq in 2003 as the application of that doctrine. The link sentence must draw out the change: from multilateral, UN-authorised action in the 1990s to pre-emptive, largely unilateral force.
questions.explanation_en: Body 2 should be written in a 'trigger → theory → practice' three-step approach. The link sentence cannot simply state 'so the US changed', but must specify 'what changed relative to Body 1'.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 2(events to include)

criteria.t: Opens the body with the 9/11 attacks as the trigger
Explains the Bush Doctrine as the doctrinal response (pre-emption, unilateralism, regime change) and the 2003 invasion of Iraq as its application
Explains what the link sentence must do: draw out the change from multilateral, UN-authorised action in the 1990s to pre-emptive, largely unilateral force

questions.stem: Write a thesis statement that answers: 'Explain the development of US foreign policy between 1991 and 2019.' (3 marks)
questions.answer: Between 1991 and 2019, US foreign policy moved from leading multilateral, UN-authorised interventions as the world's single superpower, to asserting pre-emptive and largely unilateral force after 9/11, and finally to defending a declining position against a rising China.
questions.explanation_en: The topic sentence must cover all three paragraphs, not just the first: multi-directional leadership → unilateral initiative → responding to decline. It should state the 'direction of change' in one sentence, and that sentence is the thesis.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Section Two(thesis statement row)

criteria.t: Covers the whole period 1991–2019 rather than only one phase
States a direction of change: from multilateral, UN-authorised leadership as the single superpower to pre-emptive and largely unilateral force after 9/11
Carries the argument through to the final phase: defending a declining position against a rising China

questions.stem: Explain how the three body paragraphs together answer the essay question. (4 marks)
questions.answer: Body 1 establishes the multilateral, collective-security phase of the 1990s. Body 2 explains the rupture after 9/11, when pre-emption and unilateralism displaced UN authorisation. Body 3 shows the consequences up to 2019, as China's rise, declining US soft power and a turn to protectionism ended the unipolar moment. Together they trace one line: from multilateral leadership, to unilateral assertiveness, to managed decline.
questions.explanation_en: High-scoring essays run a single thread throughout instead of writing three independent paragraphs: each paragraph is a stage in the same process of change, and the link between paragraphs must be explained rather than each one merely summarised.
questions.source: Term 4 · Yearly Assessment Notification — Body 1 / 2 / 3

criteria.t: Explains that Body 1 establishes the multilateral, collective-security phase of the 1990s
Explains that Body 2 covers the rupture after 9/11, when pre-emption and unilateralism displaced UN authorisation
Explains that Body 3 shows the consequences up to 2019, as China's rise, declining US soft power and a turn to protectionism ended the unipolar moment
Identifies the single line the three paragraphs trace (multilateral leadership, then unilateral assertiveness, then managed decline) rather than summarising each one separately
